title: Harmonic Persistent Homology
authors: Saugata Basu (Purdue University), Nathanael Cox (Purdue University)
abstract: We introduce harmonic persistent homology spaces for filtrations of finite simplicial complexes. As a result we can associate concrete subspaces of cycles to each bar of the barcode of the filtration. We prove stability of the harmonic persistent homology subspaces under small perturbations of functions defining them. We relate the notion of ``essential simplices,'' introduced in an earlier work to identify simplices which play a significant role in the birth of a bar, with that of harmonic persistent homology. We prove that the harmonic representatives of simple bars maximizes the ``relative essential content'' amongst all representatives of the bar, where the relative essential content is the weight a particular cycle puts on the set of essential simplices.

Abstract—We introduce harmonic persistent homology spaces
for filtrations of finite simplicial complexes. As a result we can
associate concrete subspaces of cycles to each bar of the barcode
of the filtration. We prove stability of the harmonic persistent
homology subspaces under small perturbations of functions
defining them. We relate the notion of “essential simplices,”
introduced in an earlier work to identify simplices which play
a significant role in the birth of a bar, with that of harmonic
persistent homology. We prove that the harmonic representatives
of simple bars maximizes the “relative essential content” amongst
all representatives of the bar, where the relative essential content
is the weight a particular cycle puts on the set of essential
simplices.
Index Terms—filtration, simplicial complex, persistent homology, harmonic homology, metric on Grassmannian, stability,
essential simplices

The main topic of this paper concerns the theory of persistent homology which is a central object of interest in the
burgeoning field of topological data analysis.
A. Background on homology theory
Homology theory is a classical tool in mathematics for
studying topological spaces. A particular homology theory

The passage from the topological space X, to the vector

homology groups). On the positive side, the homology groups
are usually computable (even efficiently computable) unlike
other topological invariants like homotopy groups – and they
retain information about many features of interest of the
original space.
The homology theory that we will deal with in the current
paper is simplicial homology theory which associates to any
simplicial complex K, its simplicial homology groups, H∗ (K).
We define simplicial complexes and their homology groups
precisely later in the paper (see Definition 1 and 4). For the
moment it will suffice to think of simplicial complexes as
higher dimensional generalizations of graphs (with no multiple
edges or self loops). A p-dimensional simplex is spanned by
(p + 1)-vertices of the complex (just as an edge in a graph is
spanned by two vertices).
A simplicial complex K is a combinatorial object (cf.
Definition 1), but it comes with an associated topological
space |K| (the so called geometric realization of K), and the
simplicial homology groups, H∗ (K), are actually topological
invariants of |K| (two simplicial complexes having homeomorphic geometric realizations have isomorphic simplicial
homology groups). The geometric realization functor | · | will
play no role in the paper but is useful to keep in mind
for visualization purposes (and also to connect simplicial
homology of a simplicial complex to the notion of homology
being a functor from the category of topological spaces to
vector spaces as stated in the previous paragraphs).

It is a basic result in algebraic topology (the so called “nerve
lemma”) that the simplicial homology groups, H∗ (Kr ), are
isomorphic to the (say singular) homology groups, H∗ (Xr ), of
X. More precisely, the nerve lemma states that the geometric
realization |Kr | is homotopy equivalent to (in fact, is a
deformation retract of) Xr (homotopy equivalent spaces have
isomorphic homology groups). Observe that for r ≤ r0 , Kr
is a sub-simplicial complex of Kr0 , and since there are only
finitely many simplicial complexes on card(X)-many vertices,
there are finitely many distinct simplicial complexes in the
tuple (Kr )r≥0 . Thus, we obtain a finite nested sequence F
of simplicial complexes, K0 ⊂ Kr1 ⊂ Kr2 ⊂ · · · ⊂ Krn
in which each complex is a subcomplex of the next. We will
refer to F as a finite filtration of simplicial complexes.
Let us return to the picture of the point-cloud X approximating an underlying manifold M . The homology of
the manifold is captured (by virtue of the nerve lemma)
by the simplicial homology groups of the various simplicial
complexes occurring in the finite filtration F. However, this
correspondence is not bijective. As one can easily visualize,
as r starts growing from 0, there are many spurious homology
classes that are born and quickly die off (i.e. the corresponding
holes are filled in) and these have nothing to do with the
topology of M . Persistent homology is a tool that can be
used to separate this “noise” from the bona fide homology
classes of M . The persistent homology of the filtration F is
encoded as a set of intervals (so called bars in the barcode of
the filtration F (cf. Definition 12)). Intervals (bars) of short
length corresponds to noise, while the ones which are long
(persistent) reflect the homology of the underlying manifold
M . The barcode of the filtration associated to X can be
used a feature of X for learning or comparison purposes. In
particular, the barcodes of two finite sets X, X 0 which are
“close” as finite metric spaces, are themselves close under
appropriately defined notion of distance between barcodes.
Such results (called stability theorems) form the theoretical
basis of practical applications of persistent homology, and we
will state new stability theorems later on in the paper.

As mentioned previously, the output of a persistent homology computation is often displayed as a “barcode”. The
barcode is considered an important invariant – a feature –
of the given filtration (or of the underlying metric space
giving rise to the filtration). We will define precisely barcodes
of filtrations later in the paper (cf. Definition 12). For the
moment it will suffice to note that the individual “bars” in
the barcode of a filtration have some intuitive topological
meaning (as explained above in the context of point-cloud
data). They correspond loosely speaking to the lifetime of
homology classes appearing in the homology of the simplicial
complexes that appear in the filtration (here we are thinking of
the ordered index set of the filtration as time). However, a new
homology class that is “born” at a certain time is defined only
modulo a certain subspace in the homology of the complex at
that time – thus identifying a bar with a particular homology
class is problematic (see Remark 3).
Additionally, often in practice there is a demand to associate
not just a homology class, but a specific cycle from the chain
group representing this class or at least a set of simplices
to each bar. This is because in applications the simplices
of the simplicial complexes of a filtration themselves often
have special significance. For instance, the vertices of a given
simplicial complex could be labelled by genes and a p-simplex
σ = (g0 , . . . , gp ) may signify positive correlation between
the genes g0 , . . . , gp (say in causing a certain disease). As an
example, in [25], the authors associate bars with representative
cycles to determine how topological features correlate with
genes that are associated with cancer biogenesis.
There have been several approaches in dealing with the
problem of associating cycles to bars of a barcode. We give a
brief survey of these techniques in Section I-H. In this paper
we describe a new approach based on the theory of harmonic
chains.

D. Stability
Stability theorems say that the persistent homology or its
associated barcode is stable under perturbations of the input
data. This makes persistent homology useful in applications,
where the data often comes from physical measurements with
their attendant sources of error. A basic body of results that
makes persistent homology theory relevant in topological data
analysis is about the stability of the persistence module [9],
[11], [10]. There are many variations of stability results in the
literature. We refer the reader to [17, Chapter VIII] and [7,
§5.6] for a survey of these results.
The Euclidean space structure on the space of chains gives
us the ability to talk about distances between harmonic homology subspaces corresponding to different sub-complexes of
some fixed ambient simplicial complex. This is important because it allows us to prove stability theorems – sub-complexes
which are close should have harmonic homology spaces which
are close under a natural metric (cf. Theorem 1 ).

E. Harmonic representatives and essential simplices

F. Weights of simplices in simple bars

As remarked above an important issue that comes up in
applications is the problem of associating an appropriately
chosen cycle representing the homology class being born at
the start of the bar (assuming that the multiplicity of the bar is
equal to one). This is because the simplices themselves in the
simplicial complex underlying the filtration often have domain
dependent meaning and if a particular simplex shows up
with non-zero coefficient in such a cycle (or more pertinently
every cycle representing the homology class), then this fact
may be considered significant from an application point of
view. This idea was formalized in [5] where the notion of
essential simplices corresponding to the bars of a barcode
was introduced. Informally, a simplex is essential relative to
a bar, if it occurs with a non-zero coefficient in every cycle
representing the bar. We generalize this notion and associate a
set of essential simplices to any simple bar (cf. Definition 23),
and then relate this notion to harmonic persistence.

the harmonicity of a representative cycle and the set of
essential simplices of a bar. If a bar in the barcode of a

G. Key Contributions
The first important contribution of the current paper is that
we prove concrete stability results for harmonic persistence
homology in the context of general filtrations of simplicial
complexes (without any underlying assumption that the
simplicial complex is approximating some Riemannian
manifold). This is very important in applications (such as in

genomics) where persistent homology methods are applied
to “relationship” data as opposed to point-cloud data from
some Rd (see [28] and also [26], [21], [22], [29] for recent
representative examples of such applications). The stability
results proved in this paper allow us to infer that harmonic
persistence theory is applicable when topological data analysis
is used outside the context of manifold learning (such as in
genomics).
The second important contribution is that we present a principled approach to representing bars in the barcode of a filtration (the key output of any persistent homology computation)
by a concrete cycle (namely, the harmonic representative).
We connect harmonic representatives with the the notion of
“essential simplices” used in prior work [5] – proving that
the harmonic representatives maximizes the essential content.
Based on this we believe that the weight vector of simplices in
the harmonic representatives of bars that we introduce in this
paper might have an important role to play in applications.
H. Prior and related work
The definition of harmonic subspaces of chain spaces of
a simplicial complex goes back to the work of Eckmann
[15]. It has been discussed in the context of statistical
inferencing and developing and studying graph Laplacians
and Hodge theory on graphs by Lim in [24]. The theory of
harmonic homology is closely related to generalized Hodge
theory and L2 -cohomology. The study of Hodge theory on
general metric spaces with motivation coming from data
analysis and computer vision was initiated in Bartholdi et
al in [1]. However, the emphasis in loc.cit. is different from
that of the current paper and is concerned more about the
connections and interplay between the generalized and the
classical Hodge theory on Riemannian manifolds. The theory
of L2 -cohomology of finite simplicial complexes was studied
from an algorithmic perspective by Friedman in [18] who
gave an efficient algorithm for computing them. This work
is also not directly to the results of this paper. Persistent
harmonic cohomology has also being mentioned before [23]
(see also [8]), but the emphasis is more on manifold-learning
rather than on general simplicial filtrations considered in
this paper. The definition of harmonic barcodes of filtrations
defined in the current paper is new to our knowledge.
Given a homology class, it is an important problem in
applications to determine a chain of simplices to represent that
class. In applications, the simplices of the complex have inherent meaning to the data being analyzed. This importance has
led to several prior means to determine a representative cycle.
Volume-optimal cycles were proposed in the non-persistent
setting in [13] and in the setting of persistent homology in
[27]. Volume-optimal cycles are cycles of a homology class
with the fewest number of simplices, and they can be found
as solutions to a linear programming optimization problem
[13]. Volume-optimal cycles focus on minimizing the size of a
cycle; an alternative approach is to determine which simplices

are necessary for the cycle and using them to represent the
cycle. Such simplices are called “essential”, and they were
introduced by Basu et. al. ([5]). In addition, the authors
present an algorithmic means to determine which simplices
are essential.
In Dey et. al. [14] the authors give a polynomial time
algorithm for computing an optimal representative for a given
finite bar (interval) in the p-th persistence diagram of a
filtration of a simplicial complex which is a weak (p + 1)pseudo-manifold (every p-dimensional simplex is incident to at
most two (p+1)-dimensional simplices). For infinite intervals,
the complex needs to be embedded in Rp+1 . The authors also
show that in other cases, the problem is NP-hard.
Finally, in [19], Gamble et. al. obtain a representative cycle
by tracking when the addition or removal of a simplex causes
a class to be born or die.
I. A few remarks about nuances
We end the introduction with a few remarks about our
work which distinguishes it from most existing literature on
persistent homology. One important point that is pertinent to
the current work is the following. Persistent homology groups
have mostly been considered in literature using coefficients in
Z/2Z (partly because of complexity reasons). In this paper we
use real/rational coefficients in order to impose and utilize an
Euclidean space structure on the chain spaces.
Another point to note is that the homology groups that
appear in the filtration along with the linear maps induced
from the various inclusions give rise to an algebraic structure,
a module over the polynomial ring in one variable, and from
the canonical decomposition of this module one obtains the
so-called “barcode” of the given filtration (see for example
[7] for an exposition). We omit the description of this
module-structure. In fact, in the next section we will take a
more direct approach and define the barcode of a filtration
directly in terms of homology – bypassing the module
structure altogether. This is not merely related to exposition –
the definition of barcodes in terms of certain sub-quotients of
homology groups (cf. Definition 11) is key to the definition
of the harmonic analog of the same (cf. Definition 15).
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section II,
we define harmonic homology spaces and state a key stability
theorem (Theorem 1). In Section III, we define harmonic persistent homology, harmonic bar codes and state two stability
theorems (Theorems 2 and 3). Finally, in Section IV, we give
a precise statement of the fact that harmonic representatives
maximize relative essential content (Theorem 4). We also
introduce the notion of weights of simplices in bars (Definition 26). In Section V we discuss future work and some open
problems. Complete proofs of all results, more discussions, as
well as several illustrative examples appear in the full version
of the paper available at arXiv preprint [2].

V. C ONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
The above results can be potentially improved in several
directions. For example, in Theorem 1, one could ask for a
more refined notion of distance between two sub-complexes
rather than that of the cardinality of their symmetric difference. It would also be interesting to test the new (harmonic)
definitions introduced in this paper in practical scenarios of
topological data analysis. For instance, determine empirically
whether the simplices carrying the highest weights for a bar
are indeed more significant in some way with respect to that
bar than the ones with lower weights.
